thread.title_full: Golden Valley picks interim chief; former chief denies allegations - NewsBreak

author: Anja Wuolu
title: Golden Valley picks interim chief; former chief denies allegations - NewsBreak
text:
By Anja Wuolu ,
18 hours ago
Matt Clark was named the interim police chief in Golden Valley following the resignation of Virgil Green.
According to a release from the city, Clark retired in May of this year after over three decades working for various police agencies in Minnesota. Most recently, he served as chief of police for the University of Minnesota Police Department.
What happened to chief Green?
In May, the then-chief Virgil Green, was placed on administrative leave. The main complaints were sharing some body camera footage with the media as well as alleged interference when another officer was being investigated for misconduct.
Per previous Sun reporting, the GVPD had responded to a 911 call of two female students fighting at Robbinsdale Academy - Highview in Golden Valley. Despite video proof of brass knuckles being involved in the incident, Assistant Principal Patrick Burrage had told officers that the weapon was not used. Green asked for felony-level investigation interference charges, but the Hennepin County Attorney's Office declined to prosecute.
The aspect of the investigation that concerned the city was that Green released the full body-worn camera footage of the incident to district officials and the press.
As the results came out and complaints were found sustained by the investigator, Green resigned.
Green argues that Minnesota Statute § 13.82, subdivision 15 grants law enforcement agencies discretion to release criminal investigative data and body cam footage when it aids law enforcement, promotes public safety or dispels unrest.
Green told the Sun Post he does not believe the investigation was fair. He stands by his choice to release body came footage and believes other complaints are based on hearsay, misunderstandings and perhaps even lies. Though he did resign officially, he claims not to have much of a choice.
"I was pressured to resign or be fired," Green told the Sun Post. "The report is damaging to my professional reputation and greatly harms my ability to secure another position. By submitting my resignation, I enabled this report to be released to the public, where I can contest its claims, implications, and inaccuracies."
Green denies misconduct
Green told the Sun Post he expected cold weather when moving from Oklahoma, but not cold people.
"I found an agency in crisis and a city leadership in conflict with its public safety leadership," Green said. "While some residents welcomed me, I had no idea I would be encountering something far worse."
The job went to Green instead of the interim chief of police, a white man who had lived in Minnesota. Several officers showed a preference for the interim chief and an exodus of police officers ensued.
"I was labeled a DEI hire," he said.
After he was chosen to lead the GVPD, the interim chief filed a discrimination lawsuit. The city settled the lawsuit for $97,500 with the interim chief and $65,000 to his attorney.
Green notes several pre-existing issues. There were George Floyd-related tensions around police racism and support — or lack thereof — of police officers by their city leaders. Tension has continued this year.
"Over the past several years, the City of Golden Valley has spent hundreds of thousands of taxpayers' dollars on DEI training," Green said. "Despite those efforts to change the culture of the workforce, the city has been struggling to hire and retain Black employees over the past several years. The city’s first DEI manager quit after a rocky start, where she was met with resistances and racism within the city."
When asked in a survey earlier this year what would give the city the single biggest improvement, staff asked for better communication, building trust, transparency, better leadership and less DEI.
Since 2021, Green said six Black city hall employees have quit their jobs for other positions because "They haven't felt supported or had opportunities to be promoted to other positions by city management."
Green said there is "a culture of fear or keep-your-head-down compliance" within the city, and this is felt most strongly by Black employees and employees of color.
"One can say that Black Golden Valley employees are left tokenized, sidelined and without real decision-making power," Green said, “proving that DEI has been more about optics with city staff than actual systemic changes."
Green said he's seen white city staff make mistakes or cause misunderstandings, but that those mistakes are usually met with additional training instead of an investigation.
"I don't want to bring up race all the time, but why am I being treated differently?" Green said. "These are all white employees. I'm the most senior Black department head and I'm being treated differently."
Green said he's never received any negative reviews or complaints prior to the investigation. In fact, he believes he had been doing a good job.
"Department employment levels are restored with diverse and dedicated professionals," Green said. "Relations with the community are strong."
Clark, the interim chief, is expected to serve for the next several months as the city searches for a permanent replacement.
“We intend to have selected a search firm, gathered appropriate input from stakeholders, and posted the police chief position before the end of the year,” City Manager Noah Schuchman said.
